title: Geometric design of highway
summary: The formulas here are few and must be exact: SSD, superelevation, grade compensation and the summit curve length. The single most examined conceptual point is that a summit curve is designed for SIGHT DISTANCE while a valley curve is designed for HEADLIGHT sight distance and COMFORT — and the reason is that centrifugal force acts upward on a summit, opposing gravity, so comfort is never critical there. Grade compensation exists because curve resistance ADDS to grade resistance, and it is not applied below a 4 percent gradient.

sections.heading: Cross-section elements
sections.body:
**Camber (cross slope)** drains water off the carriageway:

| Surface | Camber |
|---|---|
| **Cement concrete, high-type bituminous** | **1.7 – 2.0%** (1 in 60 to 1 in 50) |
| **Thin bituminous** | **2.0 – 2.5%** (1 in 50 to 1 in 40) |
| **WBM, gravel** | **2.5 – 3.0%** (1 in 40 to 1 in 33) |
| **Earthen** | **3.0 – 4.0%** (1 in 33 to 1 in 25) |

**The pattern is the point:** a **rougher and more permeable** surface needs a **steeper** camber, because water must be shed before it has time to infiltrate. A concrete surface is impermeable and smooth, so a gentle slope suffices.

**Too flat** leaves standing water — causing **hydroplaning**, pavement deterioration and, in a bituminous pavement, stripping of the binder. **Too steep** causes vehicles to **drift toward the edge**, is uncomfortable, and makes the outer wheel path wear faster. Shapes used: **parabolic**, **straight-line**, or **combined**.

**Shoulders** flank the carriageway and serve several purposes: **emergency stopping**, **lateral support to the pavement layers**, **drainage**, and space for pedestrians in the absence of a footpath. Minimum width **0.9 m** on a hill road, **2.5 m** desirable on a highway. The shoulder camber is made **steeper than the carriageway** so water shed from the carriageway continues away.

**Other cross-section elements:**

| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Kerb** | Separates the carriageway from the shoulder or footpath; **low (mountable), semi-barrier or barrier** type |
| **Median (central divider)** | Separates opposing traffic; minimum 1.2 m, desirable 5 m |
| **Footpath** | Pedestrians; 1.5 m minimum in urban areas |
| **Side drain** | Longitudinal drainage; lined in a hill cutting |
| **Cut and fill slopes** | Stability governs; benched where high |
| **Guard rail / parapet** | Where the fill is high or a drop exists — essential on hill roads |

**In hill sections, the side drain and the guard rail are not optional extras** but the two elements on which the road's survival and safety depend: the drain prevents water saturating the formation and the slope below, and the parapet is what stops a vehicle going over the edge. Both are commonly omitted or allowed to fall into disrepair, and both are cheap relative to the consequence.

sections.heading: Sight distance
sections.body:
**Three sight distances**, each for a different manoeuvre:

| Sight distance | For |
|---|---|
| **Stopping (SSD)** | Stopping before an obstruction — the **minimum** on every road |
| **Overtaking (OSD)** | Completing an overtaking manoeuvre safely |
| **Intermediate (ISD)** | A partial provision where full OSD is impossible; **ISD = 2 × SSD** |
| Head light sight distance | At night on a valley curve |

**Stopping sight distance:**

> **SSD = lag (reaction) distance + braking distance**
> **SSD = 0.278 V t + V² / (254 f)**  with **V in km/h**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Reaction time t** | **2.5 s** (IRC) |
| **Longitudinal friction coefficient f** | **0.40** at 20–30 km/h falling to **0.35** at 80–100 km/h |
| Eye height | **1.2 m** |
| Object height | **0.15 m** |

On a **gradient**, the braking distance changes because gravity assists or resists:

> **SSD = 0.278 V t + V² / (254 (f ± 0.01 n))**  — **plus** for an ascending gradient n%, **minus** for a descending one

So a **descending** gradient **lengthens** the required SSD, which is why the descending direction governs on a two-way road.

**A critical case worth remembering:**

> On a **two-way SINGLE-LANE road**, the sight distance required is **2 × SSD**, because **both** vehicles must stop.

**Overtaking sight distance:**

> **OSD = d₁ + d₂ + d₃**  (two-way road) or **d₁ + d₂** (one-way)

| Component | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **d₁** | Distance travelled during the **reaction** time (2 s) |
| **d₂** | Distance travelled during the **actual overtaking** manoeuvre (4–10 s) |
| **d₃** | Distance travelled by the **opposing vehicle** during the manoeuvre |

OSD is **very long** — of the order of 300 to 500 m at highway speeds — which is why it frequently cannot be provided.

**Overtaking zones** are provided where OSD is available, marked by signs, with a **minimum length of 3 × OSD** (desirably 5 × OSD).

**Where OSD cannot be provided, overtaking is PROHIBITED and only SSD is provided** — which in mountainous terrain is the normal situation. That is why no-overtaking zones cluster at **crests and on the approaches to blind bends**, and why hill roads are marked with continuous centre lines over long lengths.

**Sight distance on a horizontal curve — the set-back distance:**

> **m = R − (R − d) cos(θ/2)**,  where **θ = S/(R − d)** radians

with m the required clearance from the centre line of the inner lane, S the sight distance and d the distance of the driver from the centre line.

The practical consequence: **obstructions on the inside of a curve must be cleared** — parapets, cut faces, vegetation, buildings, signboards. On a hill road this means the **cut slope must be benched back at curves**, which is why hill road curves have a characteristic widened cutting.

sections.heading: Horizontal alignment
sections.body:
**Superelevation** counteracts the centrifugal force on a curve:

> **e + f = V² / (127 R)**   with **V in km/h, R in metres**

where **e** is the superelevation (as a ratio) and **f** the coefficient of **side friction**.

**The IRC design method** — and the sequence matters:

1. Compute e for **75% of the design speed**, assuming **no friction**:
 > **e = (0.75V)² / (127 R) = V² / (225 R)**
2. If e ≤ e_max, adopt it. If e > e_max, **set e = e_max** and
3. **Check that the friction required at the FULL design speed is within f = 0.15**:
 > **f = V²/(127R) − e_max ≤ 0.15**
4. If not, **restrict the speed** or **increase the radius**.

**The 75% rule exists** because superelevating for the full design speed would make the curve uncomfortable and unsafe for **slow-moving vehicles**, which would tend to slide inward on a steeply banked curve — a genuine problem on mixed-traffic roads with bullock carts and heavily laden trucks.

**Maximum superelevation:**

| Situation | e_max |
|---|---|
| **Plain and rolling terrain** | **7%** |
| **Hilly (mountainous/steep), snow-free** | **10%** |
| Hilly, subject to snow | 7% |
| **Urban roads** | **4%** |

**Minimum superelevation** equals the **camber**, so that drainage is maintained on a very flat curve.

**Ruling minimum radius** follows from e_max and f = 0.15:

> **R_min = V² / (127 (e_max + f))**

| Design speed | R_ruling (plain, e = 7%) |
|---|---|
| 100 km/h | 360 m |
| 80 km/h | 230 m |
| 60 km/h | 130 m |
| 40 km/h | 60 m |
| **20 km/h (hairpin)** | **15 m absolute minimum** |

**Extra widening on a curve** — the sum of two distinct effects:

> **W_e = W_mechanical + W_psychological = n l² / (2R) + V / (9.5 √R)**

| Component | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Mechanical widening** | **Off-tracking**: the rear wheels follow a **smaller radius** than the front, so the vehicle occupies more width than its own |
| **Psychological widening** | Drivers **keep further from the edge** on a curve, and from each other |

Both are real and both are provided. n is the number of lanes and l the wheelbase (6 m for a truck).

**Transition curves** — provided between a straight and a circular curve:

| Purpose | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Gradual introduction of centrifugal force** | Rather than the sudden jolt of entering a circular curve directly |
| **Gradual introduction of superelevation and extra widening** | Both need length to be applied |
| **Enables the driver to turn the steering gradually** | Matching the natural path a driver takes anyway |
| **Improves appearance** | Avoids the visual kink of a sudden curve |

**The spiral (clothoid) is used** because its **radius decreases linearly with length**, which is exactly the path a driver follows when turning the steering wheel at a constant rate. IRC recommends it in preference to the lemniscate or cubic parabola.

**Length of transition** — the **greatest** of three:

> **1. Rate of change of centrifugal acceleration:  L_s = 0.0215 V³/(C R)**, with **C = 80/(75 + V)** (between 0.5 and 0.8)
> **2. Rate of superelevation attainment:  L_s = e N (W + W_e)** — where N is the rate (1 in 150 for plain, 1 in 60 for hills)
> **3. Empirical (IRC):  L_s = 2.7 V²/R** for plain and rolling, **L_s = V²/R** for mountainous and steep

**Setting out the superelevation** is done by rotating the pavement about the **centre line** (usual) or the **inner edge** (where drainage requires), with the **elimination of camber** on the outer half first, then the **rotation** through the transition length.

**Hairpin bends** — the characteristic Nepali hill road feature, with **NRS 2070** parameters:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Design speed** | **20 km/h** |
| **Minimum radius** | **15 m** (at the inner edge) |
| **Minimum transition length** | **15 m** |
| **Maximum superelevation** | **10%** |
| **Maximum gradient** | **4%** — LOWER than the ruling gradient of the open road |
| Minimum length between successive bends | 60 m |
| Widening | Substantial, for off-tracking of long vehicles |

**The 4% gradient limit on a hairpin bend is the point worth understanding**, and it follows directly from grade compensation: the bend's very small radius produces **large curve resistance**, which adds to the grade resistance. A gradient a truck can manage on the open hill road becomes impassable through a 15 m radius bend, so the gradient is deliberately flattened there — even though flattening it means the road gains less height per metre and needs more bends.

sections.heading: Vertical alignment
sections.body:
**Gradients:**

| Type | Plain / rolling | Mountainous | Steep |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ruling** | **3.3% (1 in 30)** | **5% (1 in 20)** | 6% |
| **Limiting** | 5% | **6%** | 7% |
| **Exceptional** | 6.7% | **7%** | 8% |
| **Minimum** (for drainage in a lined drain) | **0.5% (1 in 200)** to 1 in 500 | same | same |

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Ruling gradient** | The **design** value, used wherever the terrain permits |
| **Limiting gradient** | Steeper, used where the terrain makes the ruling gradient uneconomical |
| **Exceptional gradient** | For **short lengths only** (not exceeding about 100 m), where unavoidable |
| **Minimum gradient** | Needed for **drainage** in a lined side drain — a road on a perfectly level grade does not drain |

**Grade compensation** — the most examined vertical-alignment concept:

> **Grade compensation = (30 + R)/R percent... ** more precisely:
> **Grade compensation = 30/R + 75/R percent, subject to a MAXIMUM of 75/R**
> and **NOT applied where the gradient is flatter than 4%**

**Why it exists.** A vehicle climbing a gradient works against **grade resistance**. On a curve it must **additionally** overcome **curve resistance** — the loss from dragging the tyres sideways as the vehicle is turned, and from the rear wheels tracking a tighter radius. **The two resistances ADD**, so a gradient a loaded truck can just manage on a straight becomes impassable on a sharp curve.

**Grade compensation flattens the gradient through the curve** to keep the total resistance within what the vehicle can deliver.

**Why it is not applied below 4%.** At such flat gradients the combined resistance is not critical, and flattening further would **create drainage problems** — approaching the minimum gradient at which the side drain will not run.

**A worked case.** For R = 50 m: 75/50 = **1.5%**. A ruling gradient of 6% would be eased to **4.5%** through the curve. For R = 15 m (a hairpin): 75/15 = 5%, so the compensation would exceed the gradient itself — which is why hairpins are simply limited to **4%** outright.

**Vertical curves** are **PARABOLIC**, not circular, because a parabola gives a **constant rate of change of grade** — the smoothest transition, and the easiest to set out by offsets from the tangent.

**Summit (crest) and valley (sag) curves — the distinction examined every sitting:**

| | **SUMMIT (crest)** | **VALLEY (sag)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Centrifugal force** | **UPWARD** — **OPPOSES gravity** | **DOWNWARD** — **ADDS to gravity** |
| Felt by the passenger as | **Relief** — reduced effective weight | **A jolt** — increased effective weight |
| **Governing design criterion** | **SIGHT DISTANCE (SSD, or OSD/ISD)** | **HEADLIGHT sight distance at night**, and **passenger COMFORT** |
| Why | The **road surface itself obstructs the view** over the crest | By day the view is unobstructed; **at night the headlight beam shoots up off the curve** |
| Comfort | **NOT critical** | **Critical** |

**So comfort is a VALLEY curve criterion and sight distance a SUMMIT curve criterion** — and a question offering "passenger comfort" for a summit curve, or "headlight sight distance" for a summit, is offering the valley criteria as distractors.

**Summit curve length**, with L the curve length, S the sight distance and N the deviation angle:

> **If L > S:  L = N S² / (2(√h₁ + √h₂)²)**
> **If L < S:  L = 2S − 2(√h₁ + √h₂)²/N**

with **h₁ = 1.2 m (eye height)** and **h₂ = 0.15 m (object height)** for SSD, and **h₁ = h₂ = 1.2 m** for OSD or ISD (the object being another vehicle).

**Both cases must be tried**, and the one satisfying its own condition adopted — a standard examination requirement.

For the **SSD case** with h₁ = 1.2 and h₂ = 0.15, the expression simplifies to **L = N S²/4.4**; for the **OSD/ISD case** with both heights 1.2 m, to **L = N S²/9.6**.

**Valley curve length** — governed by the **headlight** criterion:

> **If L > S:  L = N S² / (2h + 2S tan α)**

with **h = 0.75 m (headlight height)** and **α = 1° (beam upward divergence)**.

And by the **comfort** criterion:

> **L = 0.38 (N V³ / c)^{1/2}**, with **c = 0.6 m/s³** the allowable rate of change of centrifugal acceleration

**The greater of the two governs**, and in practice the headlight criterion usually does at higher speeds.

**Valley curves are set out as two parabolas** meeting at the lowest point (a "combined" or "double" parabola) in some practice, or as a single parabola — IRC permits the single parabola for simplicity.

**A practical note for hill roads:** providing full **OSD** over every summit is impossible in mountainous terrain, so **overtaking is prohibited and only SSD is provided**. Attempting to provide OSD would require summit curves so long that the road could not follow the terrain at all.

formulas.label: Camber by surface type
formulas.note: Rougher and more permeable surfaces need STEEPER camber, to shed water before it infiltrates.

formulas.label: Stopping sight distance
formulas.expression: SSD = 0.278 V t + V²/(254 f) ;   on a gradient use (f ± 0.01n)
formulas.note: t = 2.5 s, f = 0.35–0.40. On a two-way SINGLE-LANE road, provide 2 × SSD. Eye 1.2 m, object 0.15 m.

formulas.label: Superelevation
formulas.expression: e + f = V²/(127R) ;   IRC: design e = V²/(225R) at 75% speed, cap at e_max, then check f ≤ 0.15
formulas.note: e_max = 7% plain, 10% hilly snow-free, 4% urban. The 75% rule protects slow-moving vehicles.

formulas.label: Ruling minimum radius
formulas.note: 60 m at 40 km/h with e = 7%; hairpin absolute minimum 15 m at 20 km/h.

formulas.label: Extra widening on a curve
formulas.note: Mechanical widening is off-tracking; psychological is drivers keeping clear of the edge.

formulas.label: Transition curve length — take the greatest
formulas.expression: 1) L = 0.0215V³/(CR) ;  2) L = e·N·(W+W_e) ;  3) L = 2.7V²/R plain, V²/R mountainous
formulas.note: The spiral (clothoid) is used because its radius decreases LINEARLY with length.

formulas.label: Grade compensation
formulas.expression: = 30/R + 75/R percent, maximum 75/R ;   NOT applied below a 4% gradient
formulas.note: Because CURVE resistance ADDS to grade resistance. Hairpin bends are limited to 4% outright.

formulas.label: Summit curve length
formulas.expression: L > S: L = NS²/(2(√h₁+√h₂)²) ;   L < S: L = 2S − 2(√h₁+√h₂)²/N
formulas.note: SSD (1.2, 0.15 m): L = NS²/4.4. OSD/ISD (1.2, 1.2 m): L = NS²/9.6. Try BOTH cases.

formulas.label: Valley curve length
formulas.expression: headlight: L = NS²/(2h + 2S tan α), h = 0.75 m, α = 1° ;   comfort: L = 0.38(NV³/c)^{1/2}, c = 0.6
formulas.note: Take the GREATER. The headlight criterion usually governs at higher speeds.

formulas.label: Summit versus valley criteria
formulas.expression: SUMMIT: sight distance (force acts UPWARD, comfort not critical). VALLEY: headlight sight distance and COMFORT (force acts DOWNWARD).
formulas.note: The single most examined conceptual point in the subchapter.
